content: The law of definite proportions in chemistry states that a chemical compound always contains the same proportion of elements by mass. This principle is also referred to as the law of constant composition, which asserts that all samples of a given chemical compound have the same elemental composition. For instance, in pure water, oxygen constitutes 8/9 of the mass, while hydrogen accounts for the remaining 1/9. Together with the law of multiple proportions, the law of definite proportions forms the foundation of stoichiometry. This observation was first made by the French chemist Joseph Proust, based on experiments conducted between 1797 and 1804. In 1806, Proust articulated this principle, which might seem self-evident to modern chemists, as it is inherent in the definition of a chemical compound. However, at the end of the 18th century, when the concept of a chemical compound was not yet fully developed, this law was considered novel. In fact, when it was initially proposed, it was a controversial idea and faced opposition from other chemists, most notably Claude Louis Berthollet, who argued that elements could combine in any proportion. This debate highlights the fact that, at the time, the distinction between pure chemical compounds and mixtures was not yet fully understood. The law of definite proportions was later supported and placed on a solid theoretical foundation by John Dalton’s atomic theory, which he began promoting in 1803. Dalton’s theory described matter as being composed of discrete atoms, with each element consisting of a unique type of atom, and compounds being formed by combinations of different types of atoms in fixed proportions. It is important to note, however, that while the law of definite proportions is fundamental to modern chemistry, it is not universally applicable. There are non-stoichiometric compounds whose elemental composition can vary from sample to sample. For example, certain iron oxides can have a variable ratio of iron to oxygen atoms, resulting in oxygen content ranging between 23% and 25%. Proust’s measurements were not precise enough to detect such variations. Additionally, the isotopic composition of an element can vary depending on its source, which can cause slight variations in the mass of a pure stoichiometric compound. This phenomenon is utilized in geochemical dating, as processes in astronomical, atmospheric, oceanic, crustal, and deep Earth environments can preferentially concentrate lighter or heavier isotopes. While the effect is generally small and measurable only with modern instrumentation, it is most pronounced in hydrogen and its isotopes. Furthermore, many natural polymers, such as RNA, proteins, and carbohydrates, exhibit variability in composition even when considered pure. Polymers are generally not classified as pure chemical compounds unless their molecular weight is uniform (monodisperse) and their stoichiometry is constant. Even in such cases, they may still deviate from the law of definite proportions due to isotopic variations.
